newsitem.title: INDIA: S.Asian nations to press for closer trade links.
newsitem.headline: S.Asian nations to press for closer trade links.

text.p: South Asian foreign ministers representing one fifth of the world's people gather this week amid heightened expectations of closer trade ties but dogged by uneasy relations between old rivals India and Pakistan.

The seven-member South Asian Association of Regional Cooperation (SAARC) holds its regular council of ministers meeting in the Indian capital on December 19-20. The focus will be largely on trade and investment, Indian officials said.

The meeting, to be preceded by a gathering of foreign secretaries on December 16-18, will be the 11-year-old group's first following landmark agreements ending vexed disputes between India and two smaller neighbours, Bangladesh and Nepal.
Both accords involved water-sharing, a crucial issue in the subcontinent where most people still depend on agriculture for a living. The accords have opened up new vistas for cooperation.
But uneasy ties between foes India and Pakistan overshadow SAARC's efforts for a free trade bloc, officials said.

SAARC is comprised of the tiny Himalayan kingdoms of Bhutan and Nepal, the Indian Ocean island republics of Maldives and Sri Lanka, the world's largest democracy, mostly Hindu India, and its Moslem majority neighbours Bangladesh and Pakistan.
SAARC rules bar bilateral problems from the negotiating table, keeping the thorniest political issues to the sidelines.
Many of its 1.2 billion people live in dire poverty and would benefit from economic growth spurred by increased trade.
SAARC took the first steps towards forming a trade bloc last year with the creation of the South Asian Preferential Trade Agreement (SAPTA), vowing to form a free-trade zone by 2005.
Trade between SAARC countries accounts for only three percent of the nations' total trade.

Last month, SAARC member countries agreed to reduce tariffs on more than 1,500 products, up from 226 items covered in the first round of talks ended one year ago. "This has created a dramatic sense of expectation," senior Indian Foreign Ministry official Kamlesh Sharma said last week.
But some 4,500 products remain untouched.
India, which is by far the most populous member state and has offered about half of the trade concessions, is pressing for a third round of talks to accelerate the free trade movement.
But it has failed to win most favoured nation (MFN) trade status from arch-rival Pakistan.

India has already granted MFN status -- under which two countries undertake to give each other the maximum tariff concessions on their mutual trade which they already grant to other countries -- to all SAARC nations, including Pakistan.

India and Pakistan, which have fought three wars since independence from Britain in 1947, have said there will be no resumption of high-level bilateral dialogue, broken off in early 1994, during this week's meetings.
But both have said there will be "unofficial" bilateral sessions on the margins of the SAARC ministerial.
Bangladesh will explore the possibility of forging sub-regional trade cooperation between India, Bangladesh and Nepal, a Bangladesh Foreign Ministry spokesman said.
Water-sharing agreements between India and Nepal earlier this year and between India and Bangladesh last week have removed major bilateral irritants.
Dhaka is expecting India to do more on the trade front. "India has not liberalised its market the way we have done," the Bangladesh Foreign Ministry spokesman said on Saturday.
Sri Lanka will emphasise the need to press ahead with trade liberalisation and strengthen ties to other regional blocs, Foreign Ministry spokesman Ravinatha Ariyasinha said.
SAARC ministers will consider plans to promote intra-regional investment, avoid double taxation and harmonise customs standards, Indian officials said.
